Six reference products — two platform owners and four independents — define current user expectations.

Long-pressing a message exposes Siri actions that summarize, find items, track packages, or read flight numbers; Write with Siri composes; Smart Replies are "tuned to your writing style"; and search "ranks results by relevance and intent" rather than keywords and recency [9].

Three standard-shifts follow, and each lands on a GrapMail gap:

1.
System-level integration is table stakes.

Widgets [41][42][4], notification interactions [5], and assistant hooks [3] are how mail apps stay one tap from the inbox; GrapMail ships none of these yet [39].
2.
Trust and safety are product features, not settings archaeology.

Tracker blocking, unsubscribe, and phishing checks are marketed up front by Proton and Canary [24][26], while attack telemetry makes each more urgent [27][28]; GrapMail's audit shows none of these user-facing controls [39].
3.
Intelligence is moving on-device.

Apple exposes an on-device foundation model to third-party apps for "structured generation, summarization, and classification" [34], reachable through a native Swift API whose prompts "never have to leave" the phone [35]; Apple's own Mail uses this pattern for summaries and categories [33].

For GrapMail, this is both a differentiation path and a cost argument — on-device intelligence avoids per-request cloud spend while keeping mail content local [37].

High user visibility plus low architectural risk makes system integration the safest place to start.

### F01 — Inline reply without leaving the notification

Both apps already show notification action buttons (archive, mark read, reply, more), but the reply action currently routes the user into the app [39].

The platform mechanisms to keep the reply in the notification are standard: on Android, "the direct reply action, introduced in Android 7.0 (API level 24), lets users enter text directly into the notification" [5], within a notification that "can offer up to three action buttons that let the user respond directly from the notification" [5]. iOS documents a text-input notification action type — an action that accepts typed input from the user [45] — declared as part of the app's notification categories [46].
Why first: replying is the most frequent daily interaction, and this converts it from a context switch into an inline gesture.

Effort: S.

### F02 — Home and Lock-screen widgets

WidgetKit exists to surface glanceable, up-to-date experiences [41]; Apple's widget design guidance is built around timely, glanceable content [42].

On Android, "Glance provides a set of composables to help you build responsive widgets for the home screen with less code" [4] — a Compose-native path consistent with the existing Kotlin codebase [39].
Recommended v1 scope: unread badge, latest three messages (sender and subject), and a compose shortcut.
Beyond direct value, the widget extension is a prerequisite for two other items below (Live Activities [2]; dynamic-color widgets [7]).

Effort: M.

### F19 — Live Activities for Send Later

The apps already schedule sends [39]; a pending-send countdown with a cancel action is a textbook Live Activity — "Live Activities display your app's current data on the Lock Screen, in the Dynamic Island, in CarPlay, and on a paired Mac or Apple Watch" [2].

Implementation shares the widget extension ("add code to your existing widget extension or create a new widget extension if your app doesn't already include one") [2], with the requirement that apps "must support all presentations" [2].

Effort: S — once F02's extension exists.

### F15 — Siri, Spotlight, and Shortcuts integration

App Intents is the framework that makes app actions "discoverable by Apple Intelligence and support system experiences like Siri, Spotlight, Shortcuts, and widgets" [3] — and the same documentation calls out hardware triggers such as the Action button [3].
A first batch for GrapMail: compose-new, search, and jump-to-account intents.
This seeds the assistant experiences Apple Mail already ships (summarize, track package, find flight [9]) and is also the natural framework seam for future Focus-based account filtering.

### Finding 5: On-Device Intelligence — The Differentiation Window

2026 mail is an intelligence race, and the platform owners moved first.

Apple Mail ships "Priority Messages" — urgent mail surfaced "with AI generated summaries of the email" — and sorts incoming mail into Primary, Transactions, Updates, and Promotions, which "Apple says is done all on-device" [33].

Gmail entered what Google calls "the Gemini era": AI Overviews "summarize email threads and answer questions using natural language", Help Me Write drafts and polishes, and a new AI Inbox will "filter out unimportant emails, so you see what matters most" [43]; on mobile, summary cards appear "at the top of the email content for messages where a summary is helpful" [44].

Independents press the same buttons: Spark "summarizes long threads", produces "ready-to-send drafts in your voice", and answers inbox questions [23]; Superhuman layers Instant Reply, Auto Drafts, Auto Summarize, Auto Labels, and Ask AI across the inbox [17]; Canary ships an AI writer, thread summaries, and automatic categorization [25].
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: For GrapMail, the strategic opening is delivery locus: on-device first.

Apple's Foundation Models framework gives third-party apps "a small, on-device language model — not a general-purpose LLM, but a model optimized for structured generation, summarization, and classification" [34], exposed as "a native Swift API" whose prompts "never have to leave" the phone [35]; Apple documents its own email-summarization adapters, including safety testing in which the summarization adapter "did not amplify sensitive content in over 99% of targeted adversarial examples" [36], and developer-facing coverage frames these features as working "offline and protect[ing] user privacy" [37].
The Android analog is a Gemini-Nano-class model on current flagship silicon [38].

For an encryption-positioned provider, keeping message text on the device during inference is both a privacy story and a cost story — and competitors make clear users increasingly expect the capability itself [23][17][25].

### Privacy architecture note

The recommended stance is on-device by default; cloud by explicit consent.

The evidence base supports it technically [34][35][37] and operationally: availability windows differ by device [9][38], so feature-gating with graceful fallbacks is mandatory, and any future server-side inference should be opt-in and disclosed in plain language.

This also aligns with the privacy-first posture of the reference competitors [24][26] while matching the direction Apple itself has taken [33].

text: All six are small, self-contained, and close visible gaps without touching the intelligence layer.
F01 completes the notification-action investment that already ships on both platforms [39] using the platform-native text-input pattern [45][5].
F02 answers a zero-hit audit [39] with the two most standard surfaces in mobile mail [41][4].
F03 finishes an already-parsed capability into a working flow [39][8].
F04 and F05 close trust gaps that privacy-first competitors market as table stakes [26][29][24].
F06 removes the last server-side blocker on an already-shipped triage feature [39].
Every item is independently shippable within one release cycle, and none carries a data-model risk.
This is the competitive-parity core: each item maps to a capability that at least two reference products already market [23][17][25], or to a platform surface whose absence is conspicuous [3].
The intelligence cluster (F07–F10) shares a single model-plumbing investment and should ship as one set, gated on device capability.
The control cluster (F12–F13) shares thread-state tracking.
F15 turns on the assistant surface and unlocks Spotlight and Shortcuts alongside Siri [3][9].
F16 rides the backend's message-rendering route [40].
F17 (accessibility) and F18 (subscription cleanup) are independent and can parallelize with everything else in the wave.
Expect this wave to move the app from "competitive" to "current" against the 2026 bar.
F14 needs on-device verification before any build decision [39].
F19–F22 are platform-polish items best bundled into a single design pass timed to the next OS cycle [2][3][6][7].
F23 participates in the security telemetry trend that continues to climb [27][28].
F24–F27 each depend on earlier waves: F25 and F27 explicitly extend the intelligence layer, and F26 is the largest single scope in the list [24].
Revisit this tier after the first two waves ship, and let adoption telemetry decide the order within it.

P0 = 6, P1 = 11, P2 = 10 — 27 candidates in total.

---
The gaps are shallow, not structural.
Nothing in this roadmap requires a new subsystem.

Inline reply extends notification actions that already ship [39][5]; the unsubscribe flow completes header parsing the apps already perform [39][8]; the Live Activity reuses the send-later pipeline [39][2]; tracker shield v2 lands on a rendering route already in the backend [40]; compose assist sits on an existing rich-text editor [39].
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: That is why feasibility confidence is high — and why the P0 wave is best understood as closure work: finishing surfaces the product already committed to.
The market has converged on one capability set.
Three independent vectors arrived at the same shortlist.

Apple's Mail added on-device summaries, categories, and style-tuned Smart Reply [9][33]; Google's Gemini-era Gmail shipped thread summaries, suggested replies, and an AI inbox filter [43][44]; the independents — Spark, Superhuman, Canary — market summaries, drafts, split inboxes, and unsubscribe helpers as core [23][17][25].
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Convergence of this kind, across platform owners and independents alike, usually means the capabilities become table stakes within a product cycle or two.
The implication: the parity items in Findings 5 and 6 are time-boxed, not optional.
Privacy is the structural differentiator, if it is used.
Apple runs its mail intelligence on-device [33][34][35]; Gmail is cloud-first [43]; Proton and Canary sell privacy defaults as the product [24][26].
GrapMail already ships the privacy foundations — E2E plumbing, sessions with 2FA, human verification [39] — but has no intelligence layer at all.

An on-device-first architecture (Finding 5) converts the constraint into positioning: message content stays local, inference cost stays near zero, and the feature list matches what privacy-sensitive buyers are offered elsewhere [24][26].
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The risk is shipping nothing while rivals normalize the category.
Security is the highest-leverage trust spend.

With one in three messages malicious or unwanted and QR codes embedded in most malicious documents [27], plus phishing volume climbing through Q3 2026 [28], visible protections are a trust signal rather than an obscure setting.
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; year mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The trust release (F03–F05, F16) is cheap, testable, and directly marketable — and it lands exactly where the audit shows no user-facing controls today [39].
Sequencing follows dependencies, not desire.

Four hard gates order the roadmap: the widget extension (F02) gates Live Activities (F19) and themed widgets (F22) [2][7]; the on-device model plumbing gates F07–F10 and F27 [34][38]; the backend `?box=snoozed` route gates F06 [39]; and the backend rendering route gates F16 [40].
Everything else can reorder freely around these four.
Effort asymmetry favors starting now.

The highest-certainty work is also among the smallest: F01, F03, F04, and F06 are single-sprint items with immediate user visibility, while the intelligence items carry device-availability caveats that make them multi-quarter bets [9][38].
Shipping the P0 wave in one cycle buys credibility and the telemetry needed to de-risk everything after it.
What could invalidate this plan.

Two scenarios: platform owners absorb these capabilities into the OS itself (Apple already ships on-device summarization inside Mail [33]), eroding third-party differentiation; or user adoption of in-mail AI stalls, making Wave 2 premature.
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Both are monitored rather than predicted — the roadmap front-loads items whose value does not depend on either outcome (F01–F06, F16), and gates the rest on adoption telemetry.

Availability is uneven by device and region.

text: Signals that argue against, or qualify, this roadmap's recommendations - recorded so the plan is not read as one-sided.
Feature velocity vs. privacy stance.

Cloud-first assistants ship improvements broadly and continuously - Google moved quickly to ship AI features across Gmail [43][44] - while on-device-first designs inherit hardware and region constraints [9].
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The privacy position [24][26] is defensible, but it is a deliberate trade-off: some capabilities will arrive later, and on fewer devices.
Vendor claims are not benchmarks.
Parity estimates in Findings 1-3 rest on vendor product pages [23][24][25] corroborated by independent coverage [15][16][18][19][20][21], not standardized third-party testing.
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Treat "competitor has X" as directional until independently re-verified.
Absence evidence is snapshot-bound.

The gap list reflects a single audited commit [39]; concurrent branches or parallel work could already be closing items, which is why F14 (all-accounts view) carries a verify-first note rather than a build plan.
Quantified threat data shifts yearly.
The one-in-three malicious-message framing [27] and the QR-phishing trend records [28][29] are point-in-time measurements.
The security items (F03-F05, F16) are justified first by their small scope and visible user value, not by those statistics alone.

Apple already integrates on-device summarization, categorization, and style-tuned replies into its own Mail app [33], and OS-level absorption of that kind could erode the differentiation of third-party intelligence features (Finding 5) - making the non-AI parity and trust items the safer long-term commitments.
Wave 1 — Trust and integration release (this cycle).
Ship F01, F02, F03, F04, F05, and F06 — folding in F15 if capacity allows.
This wave closes the most visible parity gaps with the smallest scopes, and every item is independently shippable.
Telemetry to watch: reply-from-notification adoption (F01), widget installation and retention (F02), unsubscribe completions (F03), and report/block usage (F04).
Wave 2 — Intelligence core (next cycle).

Begin with model plumbing and thread summaries (F08), then categories (F07), style-tuned replies (F09), and compose assist (F10) as one gated set; run the inbox-control pair (F12, F13) in parallel; schedule F16 with the next backend rendering change [40]; F17 and F18 fit anywhere in the wave as independent scope.

text: Gate every AI surface on device capability with documented fallbacks [34][38], and route anything that could leave the device through the standing privacy review below.
_support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Wave 3 — Polish and reach (subsequent cycles).

Verify then polish the all-accounts view (F14); bundle the platform-polish items (F19–F22) into a single design pass timed to the next OS cycle [2][3][6][7]; reintroduce QR warnings (F23) as security telemetry continues to climb [27][28]; then the dependents — read receipts (F24), natural-language search (F25), action cards (F27), and finally import/migration (F26), the largest scope in the list [24].

text: Three standing rules: (1) on-device-first for anything touching message content — cloud inference only by explicit consent and clear labeling; (2) an accessibility checklist (larger text, screen-reader labels, contrast) enforced every release [31][32]; (3) a device-availability matrix maintained per platform so gating never depends on assumptions [9][38].

text: Treat the tier assignments as a snapshot: re-rank Wave 2 after Wave 1 telemetry, and revisit Wave 3 at each OS beta cycle.

The 27-item list is deliberately exhaustive; the waves are what to commit to.

text: A candidate entered the roadmap only if it passed three tests: (a) a first-party mechanism exists that can implement it natively (no WebView surfaces, per the native-only guardrail); (b) at least one credible external trigger supports its value — platform direction, competitor parity, security telemetry, or accessibility standards; and (c) it does not duplicate behavior already shipped at the audited commit.
Repository census (internal baseline).

The audit exported the `ios/` and `android/` trees of grapmail-mobile at commit `0fb5998e` (203 files: 48 Swift, 75 Kotlin) plus the backend route surface at `f9c43384`, then swept the export with roughly 30 case-insensitive capability markers (widgets, ActivityKit, App Intents, direct reply, biometrics, templates, smart replies, categories, locale configuration, dynamic color, tracker handling, and related terms).
A capability is recorded as "present" only with concrete implementation hits; "absent" means zero or trivial hits in that snapshot.
Ambiguous markers were resolved by targeted file reads — for example, the snoozed-mailbox screen's backend dependency and the notification-action wiring on both platforms [39][40].

text: External material was gathered in two waves: broad landscape and comparison queries first (features users expect in 2026, head-to-head client comparisons), then targeted retrievals for the specific platform APIs behind each recommendation, RFC 8058, the security reports, AI capability documentation, and accessibility guidance.
